To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the amounts of protein and fat in muscle are not changed in fasting rats, and that only 20% of the energy in the muscle is derived from protein.

during fasting in young rats of 30–70-day of age, the amounts of myosin and water-soluble proteins in the muscle were decreased, whereas the stroma fraction was unchanged; and that only 20 to 27% of the total calories in the thigh muscle of fasting rats was derived from protein and that the rest, from the fat.
during fasting the muscle proteins of young rats are not catabolized to any significant extent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the changes that take place in the body of the rat when it is fasted and the effects of these changes on its subsequent ability to survive and grow when fed again.
the effects of fasting on the composition and function of the muscle of young rats of different age groups.
the effect of fasting on protein and fat metabolism in young rats of various ages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

fasting for 3–4 days in young rats of various ages causes a loss of myosin and sarcoplasmic proteins in the thigh muscle and an increase of fat, but no change in the stroma or nonprotein nitrogen fractions.
fasting for several days does not result in a decrease in the total protein content of the muscle.
fasting for several days does not cause a significant loss of muscle protein or fat in young rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the muscle protein and fat are not used as a primary source of calories in the young rat during fasting, and that the ‘water-solubles’ are not used for gluconeogenic purposes.
during fasting, the muscle of young growing rats is not a source of water or nitrogen, but is a source of energy in the form of fat.

during fasting in rats of different ages there is a decrease in the amounts of the myofibrillar protein myosin and the ‘water-solubles’ in the muscle and that the decrease in myosin is due to a decrease in the amount of muscle protein and not to a breakdown of myosin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of protein that is used for calories during fasting is very small and that it is the fat stores that are mainly used.
muscle protein is not a major source of energy during fasting.
the muscle protein fractions are not affected by fasting in the same manner that liver proteins are affected, and that muscle proteins are not a major source of calories in young rats.
